question.text: Do symptoms matter when considering patients for phase I clinical trials?
question.context: Older adults (OA) with advanced cancer (AC) undergoing phase I clinical trials (PICT) have poor prognosis. There are no studies which describe symptoms experienced by OA. Retrospective chart review of PICT participants>60 years. OA were compared by age (>65 vs 60-65) and by number of symptoms (>3 vs ≤3). N = 56. Mean age = 67.09; 48.21% female. Median life-expectancy = 5 months (interquartile range = 2-9 months); 80.36% had pain; of those 64% without pain scale. Most did not have interdisciplinary professionals or hospice referrals. Older adults with>3 symptoms had more admissions (37.5% vs 14.29%; P = .0335), complications (46.43% vs 16.07%; P = .0026), and greater decline in functional status (24 participants>3 symptoms vs 8; P = .0173). There were no significant differences comparing OA by age.

medgemma_4b.clinical_reasoning: The clinical case focuses on the impact of symptoms on older adults with advanced cancer undergoing phase I clinical trials. The study found that older adults with more symptoms (defined as >3) had significantly higher rates of admissions, complications, and functional decline. This suggests that symptoms are a relevant factor in the outcomes of these patients. Therefore, symptoms matter.
medgemma_4b.critical_evidence: Older adults with>3 symptoms had more admissions (37.5% vs 14.29%; P = .0335), complications (46.43% vs 16.07%; P = .0026), and greater decline in functional status (24 participants>3 symptoms vs 8; P = .0173).
medgemma_4b.differential_considered: While the study focuses on symptoms, other factors like disease stage, prior treatments, and comorbidities could also influence outcomes. However, the study specifically isolates the impact of symptoms, making them the most relevant factor in this context.

rnj1_8b.clinical_reasoning: The data shows that older adults with more symptoms had significantly higher rates of hospital admissions, complications, and functional decline. This suggests that symptom burden is an important factor in determining patient suitability for phase I trials, as it correlates with worse outcomes and increased healthcare resource utilization.
rnj1_8b.critical_evidence: Older adults with >3 symptoms had 37.5% admissions vs 14.29% in those with ≤3 symptoms (P =.0335), and 46.43% complications vs 16.07% (P =.0026)
rnj1_8b.differential_considered: No differential diagnoses needed - this is a straightforward observational study showing correlation between symptom burden and poor outcomes in phase I trial participants

qwen3_vl_8b.clinical_reasoning: The study demonstrates that older adults with advanced cancer and more than three symptoms had significantly higher rates of hospital admissions, complications, and functional decline, indicating that symptom burden is clinically relevant in this population. Since phase I trials involve high-risk patients, symptom assessment likely impacts prognosis and trial feasibility.
qwen3_vl_8b.critical_evidence: Older adults with >3 symptoms had significantly higher admissions (37.5% vs 14.29%; P = .0335), complications (46.43% vs 16.07%; P = .0026), and functional decline (P = .0173), highlighting the clinical impact of symptom burden.
qwen3_vl_8b.differential_considered: Age-based differences were not significant, so symptom count—not age—was the key predictor of adverse outcomes, ruling out age as the primary variable and supporting symptom relevance.
